subject: chemistry
title: Dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle
key_idea: In a closed system a reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant. If a change is made, the position of equilibrium moves to minimise it. Industry chooses a compromise between yield and rate.

blocks.text: Many reactions are reversible: products can turn back into reactants. In a closed system the reaction can reach a state of dynamic equilibrium.

items.meaning: A reaction that can go in both directions, shown with the ⇌ sign.
A system where no reactants or products can enter or leave.
The state where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
How far the reaction has gone: the relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium.

items: The forward and reverse reactions are both still happening, so the equilibrium is dynamic.
The forward and reverse rates are equal.
Because the rates are equal, the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
A closed system is needed. If a product escapes, the reverse reaction cannot keep pace and equilibrium is never reached.
At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal.
Concentrations are constant, but both reactions continue.
Equilibrium needs a closed system.

blocks.text: Le Chatelier's principle lets you predict how the position of equilibrium moves when a condition is changed.

items.meaning: If a change is made to a system at dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium moves to minimise the change.

rows: Increase the concentration of a reactant
To use up some of the added reactant.
To replace some of the product removed.
To the side with fewer moles of gas
The reaction absorbs heat and so opposes the rise.
The reaction releases heat and so opposes the fall.

blocks.text: If the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides, a change in pressure has no effect on the position.

items: A catalyst speeds up the forward and the reverse reactions by the same amount.
So the position of equilibrium does not change.
It only makes equilibrium get reached faster.

diagram.alt: Pick a change to the Haber process equilibrium and see which way the position moves, and what happens to the rate and the yield of ammonia.
diagram.prompt: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Pick a change.

options.label: Increase the temperature
options.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating favours the reverse reaction.

options.label: Increase the pressure
results: Moves right (4 mol gas to 2 mol gas)
options.explanation: The right-hand side has fewer moles of gas.

options.label: Remove NH₃ as it forms
results: Decreases slightly as less product is present
options.explanation: The system replaces some of the ammonia removed.

options.label: Add extra N₂
options.explanation: The system uses up some of the added nitrogen.

options.label: Add an iron catalyst
options.explanation: Both rates rise by the same amount, so equilibrium is reached sooner but sits in the same place.

items: The position moves to oppose any change made.
More pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas.
More heat favours the endothermic direction.
A catalyst does not change the position.

blocks.text: The best conditions for a high yield are often poor for a fast rate, and the other way round. Industry chooses a compromise.

rows: Low temperature gives a higher yield (exothermic forward reaction).
About 450 °C: a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate.
High pressure gives a higher yield (fewer moles of gas on the right).
About 200 atm: very high pressure needs costly equipment and is a safety risk.
Iron, so a lower temperature can be used.

items: Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled so little is wasted.
Ammonia is removed by cooling and liquefying it, so the position keeps moving right.
The conditions balance yield, rate, safety and cost.
Yield and rate pull in different directions, so a compromise is used.
Haber process: about 450 °C, about 200 atm, iron catalyst.
Cost and safety limit how high the pressure can go.

checks.q: Explain why a closed system is needed for a reaction to reach dynamic equilibrium.
checks.a: If reactants or products could escape, the forward and reverse rates could not become equal and the concentrations would not stay constant, so equilibrium could not be reached.

checks.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH is negative. State and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium of increasing the pressure.
checks.a: The position moves to the right. There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so the system moves to the side with fewer moles of gas to reduce the pressure.

checks.q: Explain why a catalyst does not change the equilibrium yield, yet is used in the Haber process.
checks.a: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the position is unchanged. It allows equilibrium to be reached faster, so a lower temperature can be used.

extra.heading: Investigating changes to the position of equilibrium

blocks.text: The effects of concentration and temperature are investigated qualitatively, by watching a colour change in a sealed or small-scale mixture.

items: Concentration: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ [Fe(SCN)]²⁺(aq). Add more Fe³⁺ or SCN⁻ and the red colour deepens, so the position moves right.
Temperature: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue) + 6H₂O. Heat the tubes in a water bath and the blue colour deepens, so the forward reaction is endothermic.
Change one variable at a time, and compare each tube with an unchanged control.

extra.heading: Evaluating data on yield and rate

items: You may be given a table of yield at different temperatures and pressures.
Pick out where the yield is high, then say what that costs in rate, energy, equipment or safety.
Justify the conditions chosen as the best overall compromise, using numbers from the data.

blocks.text: The Contact process makes sulfur trioxide for sulfuric acid: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ mol⁻¹.

rows: Exothermic, so low temperature favours yield, but it would be too slow. 450 °C is a compromise.
High pressure favours the right (3 mol to 2 mol), but the yield is already high and high pressure costs more.
Increases the rate without changing the position.

blocks.text: Both processes show why understanding dynamic equilibrium matters: the conditions are chosen using Le Chatelier's principle.
